first_pages_text:
Abstract— In heart rate variability analysis, even a mere 1% 
presence of ectopic beats can introduce distortion in the results. 
In this study, we propose an adaptive ectopic correction method, 
taking into consideration the variability between adjacent beats 
and physiological limits, and eva luate its ectopic removal 
performance. As a result, our proposed approach demonstrates 
the potential to effectively reduce beat -to-beat variability 
without significant under- or over-interpolation, thus enhancing 
the accuracy of heart rate variability analysis. 
 
Clinical Relevance—The proposed adaptive correction 
algorithm can mitigate the distortion caused by ectopic beats, 
leading to an enhancement in the accuracy of HRV analysis. 
I. INTRODUCTION 
Heart rate variability (HRV) refers to the measurement of 
variations in the time intervals between successive heartbeats, 
providing valuable insights into autonomic nervous system 
activity, stress levels, cardiovascular health [1]. HRV analysis 
aims to evaluate the regularity and variability of heartbeats, 
contributing to our understanding of health status and 
physiological functions. The HRV analysis process involves 
several preprocessing steps, with the initial correction of 
ectopic beats, representing irregular and abnormal heartbeats, 
being the first and crucial step. A study conducted by Choi and 
Shin revealed that ectopic beats, comprising less than 1% of 
the HRV dataset, can significantly impact the analysis results 
[2]. Interestingly, in their research, interpolation techniques 
have demonstrated the ability to accommodate ectopic beats 
within a range of a few percent to 10%, depending on the 
analysis variables. 
It is worth noting that there is no universally accepted gold 
standard method for correcting ectopic beats. Researchers 
have predominantly employed deletion methods, which 
involve the straightforward removal of ectopic beats through 
rigorous thresholding, as well as interpolation methods, 
encompassing zero-order, linear, and cubic spline 
interpolations [3]. However, the deletion method introduces a 
noticeable phase shift in the HRV signal, affecting frequency 
domain parameters that are highly sensitive to such shifts [4]. 
Additionally, linear or cubic spline interpolation elevate low-
 
 
frequency components within the spectral composition of 
HRV, especially when dealing with a high number of ectopic 
beats. To address this interpolation error, it becomes necessary 
to adaptively select the appropriate number of samples for 
interpolation when correcting ectopic beats. The primary 
objective of this study is to develop a method for ectopic beat 
correction during the preprocessing stage of HRV analysis, 
employing an adaptive interpolation approach, and 
subsequently verify its feasibility. We propose an adaptive 
interpolation method based on established ectopic beat 
discrimination criteria and interpolation, as documented in 
previous studies, and evaluate the performance of ectopic 
interpolation using beat-to-beat interval data obtained in a real 
clinical setting. 
II. MATERIALS AND METHODS 
The proposed adaptive ectopic beat correction process is 
shown in Algorithm 1. In an initial screening step, we excluded 
records where the number of beats contained in the record was 
less than 50% of the maximum number of beats that could be 
present in a normal heart rate range (60-80 beats per minute; 
bpm), indicating that the heart rate detection in the record was 
not performed properly. We also excluded records that 
contained multiple missing beats in a row, such as inter-beat 
interval (IBI) > 5 s. We also excluded records that contained 
multiple missing beats in a row. 
The adaptive ectopic interpolation process is performed 
through ectopic detection, ectopic deletion, and interpolation. 
Step 1) Ectopic detection: the ectopic detection process 
checks for the presence of ectopic beats that fall outside the 
following criteria for determining a normal beat, proposed in 
a previous study [5]; 0.675hIBIn-1<IBIn<1.245hIBIn-1. 
Step 2) Ectopic deletion: if the existence of ectopic beats is 
confirmed, update the IBI after removing all beat locations that 
meet the following criteria: 0.675hIBIn-1<IBIn or IBIn>0.4 s,

Algorithm 1 Ectopic correction 
Step 0: Calculate IBI from pulse onset (tonset) 
Step 1: Ectopic detection 
if (IBIn < 0.675hIBIn-1 or IBIn > 1.245hIBIn-1) for all n is false 
terminate 
Step 2: Ectopic deletion 
if (0.675hIBIn-1<IBIn or IBIn>0.4) is true 
delete tonset, n 
update IBI 
Step 3: Interpolation 
if (IBIn<1.245hIBIn-1 or IBIn>1.5 s) at n=k 
calculate Nk=⌊IBIk/1.245hmedian([IBIm| m=k-w/2, ... , k+w/2])⌋ 
interpolate the tonset by adding Nk samples at position IBIk 
update IBI 
Step 4: Termination 
if the number of iterations reaches to the limit, otherwise go to Step 1

where IBI>0.4 s means removing IBI corresponding to more 
than 150 bpm. 
Step 3) Interpolation: The interpolation process consists of 
three steps: determining where to interpolate, determining the 
number of samples required for interpolation, and performing 
the interpolation. In the first step of determining the 
interpolation location, the IBI corresponding to a heart rate that 
is too long from the previous beat or lower than the normal 
heart rate (<40 bpm) is selected as the interpolation location 
according to the following formula; IBIn<1.245hIBIn-1 or 
IBIn>1.5 s. Then, in the step of determining the number of 
samples required for interpolation, the number of interpolation 
samples (Nk) is determined by the following formula by 
weighting the median values of w adjacent IBIs centered on 
the interpolation position. Where k is the position of the IBI to 
be interpolated; Nk=⌊IBIk/1.245hmedian([IBIm| m=k-w/2, ... , 
k+w/2])⌋ where the symbol ⌊h⌋ denotes rounded down, and w 
is set to 7 in this study. After this, the interpolation step creates 
an index to be generated after interpolation according to Nk, 
and then linearly interpolates the positions of the beats, and 
updates the IBI by finding the difference of each beat position. 
The algorithm is performed by repeating steps 1 through 3 
above and is repeated until no more ectopic is found in step 1 
or the specified number of iterations is reached. 
The proposed algorithm was validated using IBI data 
acquired from photoplethysmogram (PPG). The PPG was 
recorded with a sampling frequency of 300 Hz and a Datex-
Ohmeda S/5 monitor (GE Healthcare, Chicago, IL, USA) was 
used for signal acquisition. The pulse onsets of PPG were 
initially detected using a previously proposed adaptive 
threshold detection algorithm [6], and false detections were 
manually corrected by the proficient researchers. PPGs were 
obtained from 386 patients scheduled for routine surgery, 
however, after an initial screening process, data from 225 
patients were used in the final analysis. Ectopic removal 
performance was analyzed using Poincaré plots and 
coefficient of variation (CV). The Poincaré plot maps the 
delayed samples onto a two-dimensional plane to facilitate 
relationship analysis, and the CV is a standardized analysis of 
variation that allows the occurrence and disappearance of 
sudden changes due to ectopic beat. 
III. RESULTS 
Fig. 1 shows examples of IBI sequence before and after 
ectopic correction, where the dashed line and the solid line 
respectively shows the change in IBI before and after 
correction. As a result, it is confirmed that the proposed 
algorithm properly corrects ectopic beats without changing the 
overall signal length. Fig. 2(a) is a Poincaré plot between 
adjacent IBIs. The widespread distribution to the horizontal or 
vertical before correction (gray dots) shows that ectopic beats 
can contain very sharp changes between adjacent IBIs, while 
after correction (black dots) shows that the distribution is 
concentrated in a narrow range that means the sharp changes 
have been removed. This reduction in variability can also be 
seen in the CV change in Fig. 2(b), which shows a significant 
reduction in CV after correction compared to before correction. 
IV. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSION 
The suggested adaptive ectopic removal method has 
notably diminished the variability caused by ectopic beats and 
demonstrates potential for its application as an ectopic 
correction technique in HRV analysis process. Given that the 
ultimate objective of ectopic correction is to enhance the 
precision of HRV analysis, it is anticipated that the efficacy of 
the proposed method can be ascertained by assessing the 
accuracy of HRV analysis outcomes through its application in 
an analysis environment inclusive of ectopic beats.
